Old maps fascinate me most for their empty places. Cartographers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries often left whole regions unlabeled, or filled them with sea monsters, curling waves, and cherubs blowing wind from their cheeks. A blank space was an admission: *we don't know yet*. Today we have satellites that can read a license plate from orbit, and it's easy to forget how recently the world was mostly guesswork.

I like to imagine the mapmaker sitting by a candle, dipping a pen, deciding what to draw where knowledge ran out. Some of those guesses were wildly wrong. California appeared as an island for a surprisingly long time. Other guesses were lucky, or at least close enough to lead a ship toward a coastline that later proved real.

There's something honest about those gaps. Most of what we believe is a map with blank spaces we've simply stopped noticing. We fill the margins with confident labels about things we've never checked, and we rarely draw a little sea monster to remind ourselves where our certainty ends.

Maybe the most useful habit would be to keep a few blank spaces on purpose. When someone asks me a question I can't answer well, I'd like to say so plainly rather than inventing a coastline. A blank space, honestly marked, is more useful than a confident fiction. It tells the reader where to go exploring.

I also think the blank spaces are where the adventure lives. Nobody set out to sail toward a place already fully drawn. The unknown was the reason to leave the harbor at all, and I suspect it still is.
